Linux and traditional Unix use monolithic kernels.
Monolithic kernels run scheduling, memory management, file systems, device drivers, networking, and system-call handling together in privileged kernel space with a shared address space.
Direct function calls make monolithic kernels fast, but a faulty component can corrupt memory or crash the entire system, and the integrated codebase is harder to maintain, debug, and secure.
Linux supports kernel modules that can be added or removed at runtime while remaining in kernel space.
Microkernels generally retain low-level memory management, thread scheduling, and IPC in kernel space while moving drivers, file systems, and network stacks to user-space servers.
A crashed user-space driver can often be restarted without crashing the whole operating system.
The seL4 microkernel has been mathematically proven to behave according to its specification.
Message passing and context-switch overhead made early Mach microkernels slow, while the L4 family substantially reduced that overhead.
QNX, MINIX 3, and seL4 are popular in embedded, real-time, and safety-critical systems such as cars and medical devices.
Windows NT and macOS XNU use hybrid kernels.
Andrew Tanenbaum, identified as the creator of MINIX, and Linus Torvalds, identified as the creator of Linux, had a famous online kernel-design exchange in 1992.
Next.js supports deployment to GitHub Pages through static export using output: 'export'.
Next.js defaults to server-side features requiring Node.js runtimes such as Vercel.
Astro generates static HTML by default.
Astro on GitHub Pages offers fast builds, minimal browser JavaScript, zero hosting costs, and no vendor lock-in.
Astro can also be deployed to Vercel for server-side rendering or edge functions.
GitHub Pages hosts only static files and cannot run a Node.js server.
Next.js can use output: 'export' for GitHub Pages, but its API routes, server-side rendering, and image-optimization backend do not work there without extra configuration.
Vercel was built specifically by the creators of Next.js and handles its server-side features with zero setup.
Astro uses an islands architecture and ships zero JavaScript by default.
Astro supports HTML and Markdown along with React, Vue, and Svelte components.
Astro builds to static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
GitHub Pages hosting is free and tied directly to the code repository.
Deploying Astro to GitHub Pages requires a GitHub Actions build-and-deploy workflow.
Astro can also be hosted on Vercel, Cloudflare, or Netlify.
The Vercel, Cloudflare, and Netlify hosting option offers one-click Git deployment, automatic pull-request preview URLs, built-in analytics, a global edge CDN, and a generous free tier.
